sections.heading: WELCOME BACK!
sections.text: Or for those who are joining us for the first time, welcome aboard! Prowlers & Paragons Ultimate Edition (or P&P), is the revised, expanded, and much-improved edition of the original Prowlers & Paragons. P&P is a tabletop roleplaying game with a rules-light engine that blends narrative task resolution and concrete combat rules to create a unique system designed to emulate four-color superhero comics. Great, so what does that mean to you? P&P is a tabletop roleplaying game. If that one threw you for a loop, you’re in for a treat. Skip to the next section, What is Roleplaying, to see what you’ve gotten yourself into. P&P is rules-light. As far as roleplaying games go, P&P is a simple game with streamlined rules. Once you know how things work, you should be able to play without ever opening the book. Although simple rules might not work for every genre, this is a game about superheroes, and light rules are less troublesome when mimicking comic-book action rather than real-world physics. P&P blends narrative task resolution and concrete combat rules. For the most part, P&P relies on what’s become a signature element in many narrative game systems; rather than telling you what happens, the rules help you figure out who gets to describe what happens. However, P&P isn’t a purely narrative game, especially not when it comes to combat. The combat rules are more defined, adding a tactical element to ensure that players feel like superheroes rather than comic book writers. Last, P&P is designed to emulate four-color superhero comics. This game tries to capture the reality of the superhero genre rather than simulate the real world and its pesky physical laws. P&P is a game about superheroes, about the heroic things they do, and the heroic burdens they shoulder. Mundane matters get little to no attention. While the game includes elements designed to encourage good roleplaying, the focus isn’t on the emotionality or psychology of being a superhero. To be perfectly clear, P&P isn’t a deep and cerebral game. It’s a game designed to let you play stories about superheroes who save the world and beat the snot out of supervillains who richly deserve it. Like so much of the genre, P&P is a gleefully unapologetic exercise in escapism and heroic wish fulfillment.

sections.heading: WHAT IS ROLEPLAYING
sections.text: If you’re reading this, you probably already know the answer to that question. Nowadays, many people have played or watched someone else play a tabletop roleplaying game, whether live or online. And many more have been introduced to the basic idea of roleplaying games through video games and massively multiplayer online roleplaying games such as the sadly defunct and still sorely missed City of Heroes (we promised ourselves we wouldn’t cry). A tabletop roleplaying game is one in which a group of people collectively create a story. When you play P&P, you take on the role of a superhero (a Hero) in the imaginary world in which the game takes place. You and your fellow players create your own Heroes and control them in the game. You’re usually cooperating with rather than competing against your fellow players because there’s no winning or losing. You play for the fun of it rather than to beat your opponents or win the game. Again, this should be familiar to anyone who’s ever played a massively multiplayer online roleplaying game. While most of the people playing P&P — or any tabletop roleplaying game — play a specific Hero, one person takes on the role of the gamemaster (or GM). The GM has three responsibilities. First, the GM comes up with the stories in which the Heroes become involved and creates the supervillains and other characters with whom the Heroes interact. Second, the GM acts as the narrator of the story and plays these non-player characters (or NPCs) during the game. Third, the GM acts as the moderator of the game and decides when and how to apply the rules. P&P takes place in the minds of the people playing the game. There are no pieces to move around a board, no cards to shuffle and hand out, nothing like that. Instead, when the game begins, the GM sets the stage by telling the players where their Heroes are and what’s happening around them. The players imagine themselves in that situation and tell the GM what they do in return. The GM describes what happens in response, the players react to that, and so on. There are times when you have to roll dice and consult the rules, but most of the time, the game involves nothing more than this back-and-forth conversation between the GM and the players as they make their way through the story. Games usually last three to six hours, but some folks enjoy longer sessions. A game session normally ends when the story concludes, but many stories take more than a single session to finish. As a result, game sessions often end when GM feels the group has reached a logical stopping point.

sections.heading: GLOSSARY
sections.text: In the spirit of the source material that inspired this game, we sometimes use comic-book lingo in place of common roleplaying terms. Other times, we stick with traditional roleplaying game terminology, or we use everyday words to mean something specific. Here’s what we mean by the following terms. Extra: A character run by the GM who isn’t a Villain, Foe, or Minion. Extras can be mundane civilians of any stripe, good, evil, or anywhere in between. They can also be characters with powers who aren’t enemies, such as other superheroes or neutral parties who just happen to have superpowers. Foe: A henchman, lieutenant, or minor enemy who poses more of a threat than a Minion but isn’t as competent or dangerous as a Villain. Like all enemy characters, Foes are run by the GM. GM: An abbreviation for gamemaster, the person who runs the game. Half: Whenever we refer to half of an odd number (or half of an odd number of dice), always round up, regardless of the context. For example, half of 3d is 2d and half of 1d is 1d. Hero: A character — presumably a superhero — run by a player. A player may occasionally control other characters, but only their main character is considered a Hero. Issue: A single session of gameplay. Just like every issue of a well-written comic, every issue of P&P should start with a bang and end with something that leaves the players hungry for more. Minion: Minions are generic enemies like gang members, killer robots, ninjas, or toughs, characters who only pose a threat to the Heroes in groups. Like all enemy characters, Minions are run by the GM. NPC: Short for non-player character, this is any character run by the GM. Page: Often called a round or a turn in other roleplaying games, a page is a brief unit of in-game time that represents a few seconds of combat or any other fast-moving scene. It represents roughly one page of a comic book or a few moments of an action sequence in a movie or show. Scene: A variable unit of in-game time roughly equivalent to one chapter of a book or one scene of a movie or show. Scenes normally revolve around a specific action, event, goal, location, or task. Series: Often called a campaign in other roleplaying games, a series is a collection of stories that typically involve the same Heroes and unfold in chronological order. While this term usually refers to an ongoing campaign that can last months or even years, that doesn’t have to be the case. As in the comics, you can instead have a one-shot series, which is really just a single story, or a mini-series that involves a limited number of stories connected by an overarching metaplot. Story: Often called an adventure in other roleplaying games, a story is a single tale that involves the Heroes and has a distinct beginning, middle, and end. Unlike in a traditional story, however, the collaborative nature of roleplaying makes it entirely possible that the story that gets told over the course of the game turns out to be very different than what the GM originally had in mind. Travel Power: A type of Power that lets you move faster than a normal person. Villain: A competent, dangerous, or important enemy who is at least as powerful as the Heroes if not much more so. Like all enemy characters, Villains are run by the GM. Xd: This indicates a number of ordinary 6-sided dice. For example, when you roll 8d, you roll 8 dice of the ordinary 6-sided variety. Modifiers of +Xd or -Xd require you to add or subtract that many dice before rolling them. For example, a −2d penalty means you roll 2 fewer dice than normal.
